name: PackServe: SLO-Aware Request Scheduling for Agentic LLM Serving at Scale
problem: Agentic workloads reuse KV cache across long shared prefixes, so naive request consolidation onto fewer instances trades away cache locality and prefill/decode interference, wrecking both SLO attainment and GPU efficiency at the same time.
mechanism: Use compact white-box models to PREDICT latency under prefill/decode interference, then pack requests onto fewer serving instances subject to preserving KVC reuse and the token-level SLO — explicitly trading unused latency headroom for higher per-instance throughput. The white-box predictor is what makes safe packing possible without over-provisioning.
speedup_reported: Per the arXiv abstract, on 64 NVIDIA H20 GPUs: up to 16.8% and 24.6% fewer GPU-hours than state-of-the-art schedulers under 30-ms and 50-ms TPOT targets respectively, while still meeting the target TPOT objectives. Note this is a COST/footprint reduction at equal latency, not a raw throughput multiple, and the hardware is H20 — a memory-capacity-and-bandwidth-constrained part, so read the result as evidence that scheduling efficiency can substitute for buying more accelerators.
notes:
Recorded adoption as 'unknown' rather than 'in-production' even though the abstract says the authors deployed it in their own environment: a paper's claim of internal deployment is not evidence a reader can use, and I could not verify a public repo or release. Venue deliberately 'arxiv-preprint' — the arXiv comment states only a page and figure count, with no venue. This is the clearest current example of the packing-vs-cache-locality tension that post-2024 agentic serving is fighting.
